title: On the large deviations behavior of acyclic networks of queues
contribution: Gives a large-deviations calculus for single-class acyclic networks of G/G/1 queues: the assumptions on arrival and service processes are shown to survive passing through a queue, superposition and deterministic splitting, so waiting-time and queue-length tails at every node follow by induction, together with their most likely paths.
problem_entry: {SD} Tail probabilities in packet networks; the closest prior G/D/1 departure result rests on assumptions about its input that are not re-verified for the departure process, so it cannot be chained node to node (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Impose LD Assumptions B and C, prove that departure, superposition and splitting preserve them, and induct over the acyclic network; the most likely path is read off the optimizer of each rate-function problem (pp. 3, 7, 9, 20-22).
assumptions: Acyclic graph in which paths meet at most once; single class; FCFS; stationary, possibly dependent arrivals; iid service; deterministic routing fractions; implicit stability (pp. 6-7). One-sided LDP with strictly convex rate functions (admitted as technical) and sample-path lower bounds from mixing (pp. 8-9). No data.
proof_devices: Waiting-time LDP taken from the literature ('This result is not new') (Theorem 4.1, p. 10)
Distributional-law relation from queue length to waiting plus service time, valid without the renewal assumption in the LD setting (Eq. 28, pp. 12-13)
Departure-process LDP by sample-path upper and matching lower bounds; most likely path read off the optimizer (Theorem 5.4, pp. 16, 20-21)
One-sided Varadhan lemma: the departures' log-MGF as a convex dual, so the induction can continue (p. 22)
Burke's theorem recovered for M/M/1 in the LD regime (p. 4)
Palm and stationary versions of a point process have the same LD behaviour (Theorem 6.4, pp. 30-31)
Closure under superposition and deterministic splitting (pp. 26, 35-36)
experiments: One Matlab example of two tandem queues with deterministic servers and two-state Markov-modulated arrivals: theta1* = -9.47; departures smoother than arrivals; no large queue at the second node. No simulation (pp. 38-40).
positioning: Extends the inductive G/D/1 approach of its ref. [16] to continuous-time G/G/1 networks while doubting that [16] can be applied inductively; self-contained rather than relying on [14]'s technical result; two related works noted as seen only after submission (pp. 2-3).
writing: Contributions framed as a calculus of network operations; candid credit ('This result is not new', p. 10) and doubt about prior work ('not very clear to us', p. 2); works seen after submission acknowledged (p. 3); a worked example with most-likely-path figures (pp. 37-40).
limits_future: Single class, acyclic, FCFS, paths meeting at most once (p. 6). Open problems: feedback, several traffic types, and scheduling policies chosen in the LD regime (p. 40).

method_links.note: Optimization is the analytic language rather than a solved model: rate functions are infima over empirical-rate paths whose minimizers are the most likely paths, and convex duality returns the log-MGF the next node needs. No LP, conic or MIO class and no solver. Bears on Inner Tension T3.
Written with a student co-advised with Tsitsiklis (Paschalidis, PhD 1996) and with the co-adviser himself (04-mentorship A.2).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Closure calculus for decomposition
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Departure, superposition and deterministic splitting preserve Assumptions B and C, so each queue is analysed alone by induction. The same move recurs in the 2015 robust queueing paper S119 (card c15), and both papers have a Burke-type theorem.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: most likely path as an optimizer
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The path that realizes a rare event is the optimizer of the variational problem behind the rate function; it is drawn for the departure process and for the tandem example. Recurs in S187.

transferable: To analyse a network inductively, pick an assumption class for input processes and prove that every network operation (departure, superposition, splitting) maps the class into itself. One single-node theorem plus induction then covers every node (pp. 3, 9).
Before chaining someone else's single-node result, check that its output satisfies the conditions it requires of its input, and say so in print if it does not (p. 2).
Present a rare-event result together with its most likely path: the empirical arrival and service rates over the busy period that cause it (pp. 20-21, Fig. 6).
coauthors: Ioannis Ch. Paschalidis, John N. Tsitsiklis

quotes.text: our approach provides a calculus of acyclic networks since we will be able to determine the large deviations behavior of each individual queue inductively
It is an interesting open problem to derive similar results for network models that have feedback and accommodate more than one type of traffic.

title: From valid inequalities to heuristics: A unified view of primal-dual approximation algorithms in covering problems
contribution: Proposes a generic primal-dual algorithm for 0-1 covering problems whose worst-case ratio equals the strength of the valid inequalities it uses, proves the bound tight, and recovers many known approximation and integrality results by computing strengths.
problem_entry: {IO+LO} Polyhedral combinatorics can judge valid inequalities only by computational experience, and primal-dual analyses are problem specific and give no design insight. Aim: design approximation algorithms when better formulations are available (p. 1).
key_idea: At each stage, add a valid inequality, raise its dual, fix the cheapest variable and recurse; finish with reverse deletion. The ratio equals the strength of the inequalities (max a.w/b over minimal solutions), so algorithm design becomes inequality design (pp. 2-4).
assumptions: min cx, Ax >= b, x binary, with A and c nonnegative and a nonnegative objective (pp. 1-2). Reducible formulations (fixing a variable keeps the instance in its class) make strength computable on the original instance (p. 4). No data.
proof_devices: Backward induction over the primal-dual stages, using minimality: Z_H <= lambda sum y_r b_r <= lambda Z_D (Theorem 1, pp. 3-4)
Tightness instance: a cost vector built from the extreme minimal solution forces Z_H >= lambda(1-eps) IZ (Theorem 2, p. 4)
Geometric slab picture: the thinnest slab between ax = b and ax = lambda b that holds the minimal solutions (pp. 3-4)
Reducibility (Definition 2, p. 4), and enlarging the class to weakly supermodular functions to regain it (p. 10)

Strength calculations: multicut 1 and cut 2(1-1/n) for MST (p. 5); row-sum f (Theorem 5, p. 5); 4 log|V| via Erdos-Posa (pp. 5-6); uncrossable functions 2(1-1/l) (Theorem 8, pp. 6-7); contra-polymatroids 1 and k (Theorems 9-10, p. 8); set-covering matrices (Theorems 11-15, pp. 8-9)
Multiphase extension with a harmonic factor, by induction on b_max (Theorem 16, pp. 9-10); 2H(f_max) for weakly supermodular cut covering (Theorem 17, p. 10)
positioning: Builds on Goemans-Williamson and Williamson et al. (primal-dual with reverse deletion); separates its strength from Goemans's TSP notion; claims the best known bound in most cases (pp. 1, 3).
writing: Two numbered contributions, one conceding lower efficiency (p. 2); a geometric figure before the tightness theorem (pp. 3-4); remarks after the theorems; three numbered open problems at the end (p. 11).
limits_future: Algorithms less efficient than the known ones (p. 2). Constructing the minimal sets is open for uncrossable and weakly supermodular functions (pp. 7, 10). Open problems: least-strength inequalities, coordinating choices across stages, and strength under instance restrictions (p. 11). Fractional covering in stochastic scheduling deferred to Teo's thesis (p. 11).

method_links.note: The IO form of formulation first: the valid inequalities are designed first, and the algorithm and its guarantee follow from the dual variables the algorithm builds. The boundary is printed as a tightness theorem and open problems. Sits on the strong-formulation side of Tension T4.
A student paper of the IO lineage (Teo, PhD 1996, 04-mentorship B.6); the extension is carried into his thesis.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: subsume the incumbent as a special case
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Recovered as strength calculations: Kruskal, the Hall-Hochbaum and Bertsimas-Vohra row-sum bound, Bar-Yehuda et al.'s 4 log|V|, Williamson et al.'s 2-approximation and Goemans et al.'s cut-covering bounds.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: bound, constructive heuristic, provable ratio, tightness instance
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Theorem 1 bounds the heuristic by strength, Theorem 2 builds the tight cost vector, and Remark 3 makes each application's bound essentially tight.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: From-X-to-Y titles naming the transplant
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: 'From valid inequalities to heuristics' names the transfer from polyhedral combinatorics to approximation algorithms; a 1998 instance, earlier than those in card c18.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: re-derive classical theorems with the new device
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Integrality of the multicut and constrained contra-polymatroid polyhedra, Kruskal's algorithm, and optimality on consecutive-ones matrices all follow from strength-1 inequalities.

transferable: Turn approximation-algorithm design into inequality design. Define the strength of a valid inequality against minimal solutions and prove ratio <= maximum strength by induction over the primal-dual stages. Each new problem then needs only a strength calculation (pp. 3-5).
Show the bound is not an artefact of the analysis. Build a cost vector from the extreme minimal solution so that the algorithm attains lambda(1-eps) (p. 4).

Use reducibility, under which fixing a variable keeps the instance in its class, so a property checked once holds at every stage. Enlarge the class (weakly supermodular rather than proper functions) when that is what restores reducibility (pp. 4, 10).

quotes.text: Theorem 1 reduces the construction of good approximation algorithms to the design of valid inequalities of small strength.
Though the algorithms constructed by this framework are not as efficient as the known ones, the analysis of the algorithms is considerably simpler.

title: Optimization of multiclass queueing networks with changeover times via the achievable region approach: Part II, the multi-station case
contribution: Develops new constraint families for multi-station multiclass queueing networks with changeover times (flow conservation at aggregated queues, network work-decomposition laws, convex changeover constraints and PSD moment constraints). They give LP, SDP and convex lower bounds, an N-step Klimov-type bound and two heuristic policies.
problem_entry: {SD+LO+CP} Multi-station MQNETs have no exact analysis and are intractable to optimize, so computable bounds are needed. The existing achievable-region tools exclude changeovers or multiple stations, and potential functions give no physical insight (pp. 1, 3).
key_idea: Lift equilibrium relations into constraints on conditional moments, add PSD constraints, and project back onto mean queue lengths. The potential-function constraints turn out to be the flow-conservation law L- = L+ (pp. 3, 5, 8-11).
assumptions: Single-server stations; Poisson arrivals; exponential service; Markovian routing with I-P invertible; general changeover times; steady state under a stable policy (rho < 1 per station necessary, not sufficient) (pp. 4-5). Flow conservation needs only a finite first moment of the total queue length (p. 11). Synthetic instances only.
proof_devices: Lift-bound-project plan credited to Lovasz-Schrijver (p. 5)
Flow conservation L- = L+ for aggregated S-queues; Palm probabilities turned into time-stationary ones via Papangelou's theorem and stochastic intensities (Theorem 3, pp. 9-10)
Closed formulas for all the higher-order constraints that potential functions generated recursively (Corollary 1, Remark 2, pp. 10-11)
Network work-decomposition laws; workload bounds stronger than Bertsimas-Paschalidis-Tsitsiklis 1994 and exact in the single-server case (Theorem 4, Corollary 3, pp. 12-13, 16)
PSD condition [1 z'; z Z] >= 0 on first and second moments (Theorem 6, pp. 20-21)
N-step bound from Klimov's adaptive greedy, valid by LP duality (Theorem 7, pp. 22-23)
Policies: Klimov indices on a fictitious pooled server; a randomized decentralized rule from a truncated LP (pp. 26-28)
experiments: Limited experiments, run by Sethuraman; no solver or run time stated. Two-station line: Z_CONVEX vs the best of 4 simulated priority rules (rho = 0.9: 3.05 vs 17.12; the bound is weak). Rybko-Stolyar network: Z_LP2 and Z_SD2 vs a tuned LBFS rule (rho = 0.983: 80.766 / 81.093 / 85.643; both bounds strong). One station with a second-moment objective: LP 89.332 vs SDP 725.855 vs optimal 1166.362 (rho = 0.975), so the SDP is not exact. Policies untested (pp. 23-26, 30).
positioning: The achievable-region approach from Coffman-Mitrani 1980 and his 1995 survey; constraints placed against Bertsimas-Paschalidis-Tsitsiklis 1994, Kumar-Kumar 1994 and Klimov 1974; the limits of earlier tools listed (pp. 2-3, 10-11).
writing: Numbered contributions in the abstract and introduction (pp. 1, 3); 'support the thesis' framing (p. 3); Table 3 lists every bound with its class and size (p. 22); no concluding section (pp. 26-30).
limits_future: Z_CONVEX is weak in heavy traffic (p. 24) and the SDP is not exact (p. 26). No optimal policy for networks, and the index policy's stability is unresolved (p. 26). The finite-buffer LP is not a formal bound (p. 27). Policies untested. An exact relaxation for the special case is called interesting future work (p. 26).

method_links.note: SW1 in practice: stochastic scheduling written as LP, SDP and convex programs over a relaxed achievable region. Klimov's indices, read off the LP dual, give both the N-step bound and an index policy, and the boundary is printed. Partly answers the 1995 survey's open problems on SDP relaxations and network policies, which 01-publications SW1 records as followed only in part.

The relaxation bound is set against the incumbent heuristic (best simulated priority rule, tuned LBFS, a known optimal policy) instead of a solver certificate. No solver versions, run times or replication counts.
One student (Nino-Mora) carries the programme through his PhD and postdoc, and a second student (Sethuraman) runs the computations; the work is split into Part I and Part II papers.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: physical origin of an algebraic device
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Constraints found by the potential-function method are shown to formulate the flow-conservation law L- = L+, which yields closed formulas for the whole hierarchy. Recurs in S212.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: PSD moment-matrix strengthening carried across domains
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Covariance PSD constraints on queue-length moments (Theorem 6), called a new application of SDP in stochastic optimization and tested in Tables 5-6.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: policy read off a relaxation
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Klimov indices of a fictitious pooled single server, and a randomized decentralized service rule from the z variables of a truncated finite-buffer LP; neither is tested.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: staged companion papers from one model
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Part I (single station, S212) and Part II (multi-station) share the model, the constraint families and the person who ran the experiments.

transferable: Write conservation laws at Palm epochs, then convert each Palm expectation into a time-stationary one with Papangelou's formula. All constraints then live on one set of variables (pp. 9-10).
When a family of constraints was found algebraically, look for the physical law it encodes. The law can give closed formulas for the whole hierarchy (pp. 3, 10-11).
Add the PSD condition [1 z'; z Z] >= 0 whenever the variables are the first and second moments of one random vector (Theorem 6, p. 20).
Test a relaxation on an instance whose optimal policy is known, so that non-exactness is shown, not assumed (Table 6, pp. 25-26).

quotes.text: Our objective in this paper is to support the thesis that the achievable region approach is an effective tool for solving hard performance optimization problems.
Also, since we know that the simulated policy is optimal, we can also conclude that the semidefinite relaxation we consider is not exact.

title: Asymptotically optimal algorithms for job shop scheduling and packet routing
contribution: Gives algorithms for job-shop scheduling and packet routing whose makespan exceeds a fluid or multicommodity-LP lower bound only by a lower-order term independent of the number of jobs. They are therefore asymptotically optimal on every instance with many jobs, without probabilistic assumptions.
problem_entry: {IO+SD+LO} Job-shop makespan is NP-hard and hard even at 10x10, and packet routing adds path selection. The paper enters by combining fluid control of queueing networks with LP-rounding approximation, in the many-jobs regime (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Solve the fluid relaxation in closed form (makespan = maximum congestion C_max), then follow its proportional effort with a synchronization algorithm that processes fixed batch counts per window. For path selection, use a multicommodity LP relaxation (pp. 7-12, 17-19).
assumptions: Deterministic instances: integer processing times, n_i jobs of each type present at time 0, no arrivals, nonpreemptive processing; unit-time edges for packets; no probabilistic assumptions; the bound's constants depend on processing times (pp. 2, 4-5).
proof_devices: Fluid control problem solved in closed form: congestion gives the lower bound, and a processor-sharing-like construction attains it (Proposition 2, pp. 7-8)
Synchronization algorithm with window length R + U_max, R chosen to balance the error terms (pp. 8-12)
Tagged-job delay bound over at most J_max stages (proof of Theorem 1, pp. 10-11)
Proportional case: C_max + O(1) (abstract p. 1; p. 13)
Analytical comparison with Sevast'janov's bound via a job-count threshold (Proposition 3, pp. 13-15)
Multicommodity-flow LP lower bound, and packet-routing synchronization with a final sequential clean-up (Proposition 4, Theorem 3, pp. 17-22)
experiments: Three variants on the Muth-Thompson 10x10 instance with N jobs per type, up to 2,500 (Figs. 1-2; values lost in extraction). The no-idling 'variable Omega' variant, which has no theorem, is within 1% of the lower bound for N >= 500. No run times, other baselines or packet-routing tests (pp. 13-15).
positioning: Joins fluid control (Avram-Bertsimas-Ricard, Luo-Bertsimas, Weiss) with LP-rounding approximation (Shmoys-Stein-Wein and successors). The closest rival, Sevast'janov's geometric algorithm, is called more complex and its bound argued weaker. Contrasted with Karp's probabilistic asymptotics (pp. 2-4).
writing: Algorithms-journal style, with each theorem followed by intuition; simplicity claimed over the closest rival (p. 3); the conclusion reads the result as dynamics dominating combinatorics at scale (p. 22).
limits_future: The additive term depends on processing times (p. 4). The routing clean-up step is inefficient (p. 19). The abstract's 'within 1% of optimality even for moderately sized problems' rests on N >= 500 jobs per type and on the variant without a theorem (pp. 1, 13). No future directions are stated (p. 22).

method_links.note: A combinatorial problem owned by scheduling is relaxed into a fluid control problem (a continuous LP) solved in closed form and, for routing, into a polynomial-size multicommodity LP; the schedule is built from the relaxation.

Quality is reported as distance to the relaxation's lower bound, not certified by an exact solve. The best variant is not the one with the theorem, and the incumbent (Sevast'janov) is compared by bounds only.
A co-advised student of the SD lineage (Gamarnik, co-advised with Tsitsiklis per 04-mentorship A.2) keeps collaborating after graduating.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: asymptotic optimality as the warrant for a simple heuristic
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Asymptotic optimality holds instance by instance with no probability model, explicitly contrasted with Karp's probabilistic analysis; the experiments ask where the regime begins.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: relaxation-centred IO
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The fluid and multicommodity relaxations serve as bound, design template and yardstick for the schedules.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: fluid relaxation from queueing control used for deterministic scheduling
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A device built for multiclass queueing networks is carried into deterministic job shops and packet routing; the conclusion reads it as dynamics dominating combinatorics at scale.

transferable: For a scheduling problem with many identical jobs, solve the fluid relaxation (proportional sharing) in closed form and convert it into a periodic discrete schedule with fixed batch counts per window. Choose the window length to balance the two error terms (pp. 7-12).
Prove asymptotic quality instance by instance, with no distribution. Then measure on a classical hard benchmark at what size the regime begins (pp. 4, 13).
When the incumbent's code is not at hand, compare guarantees analytically: derive the job-count threshold below which your bound beats its bound (Proposition 3, pp. 13-15).

quotes.text: Unlike asymptotically optimal algorithms that rely on probabilistic assumptions, the above algorithm makes no probabilistic assumptions, and it is asymptotically optimal for all instances with a large number of jobs (packets, respectively).
as the number of jobs increases, the combinatorial structure of the problem is increasingly less important, and as a result, a fluid approximation of the problem becomes increasingly exact.

title: Optimal control of execution costs for portfolios
contribution: Extends the Bertsimas-Lo best-execution dynamic program to portfolios with a multivariate linear-percentage price-impact model. It is solved in closed form without constraints; no-sales constraints are handled by a re-solved static QP. The model is calibrated on proprietary 1996 trade data that show significant cross-stock impact.
problem_entry: {AP+SD} Managers trade lists of stocks within short horizons, and single-stock execution models miss cross-stock impact, whose sign is an empirical question. Problem: minimize the expected cost of buying fixed blocks within T periods (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: A stochastic DP with temporary percentage impact, linear in the dollar trades of all stocks and in an AR(1) information vector. The value function is quadratic and the policy linear, coupling all stocks unless A is diagonal. Constraints are handled by a static QP re-solved each period (pp. 3-7).
assumptions: Temporary linear percentage impact, A positive definite, stationary AR(1) information, expected-cost criterion (pp. 2-3). Data: ITG's 1996 NYSE trades, TAQ quotes and S&P 500 ticks for the 25 most-traded large caps (downward-biased impact admitted); 2,069 half-hourly returns (pp. 7-8).
proof_devices: Backward Bellman recursion with quadratic value and linear policy; coefficients in a web appendix (Eqs. 8-9, pp. 4-5)
Counting where the class ends: 3^k piecewise-quadratic pieces under nonnegativity, 3^20 = 3,486,784,401 at T = 20 (p. 6)
Static approximation: a convex QP over the remaining horizon from the current state; the first decision is implemented and the problem re-solved (pp. 6-7)
No-arbitrage condition (positive definiteness) imposed in estimation to keep the problem convex (pp. 11-12)
experiments: 25 SAS regressions: R2 0.052-0.440; 193 of 625 t-statistics and 18 of 25 own-impact terms significant. The unconstrained impact for one stock is about 20 cents/share, judged unacceptably high; the constrained fit costs about 5% more squared error. Monte Carlo with 10,000 replications per setting against naive equal lots: the optimal strategy wins in all but two cases (Table 6 values not extracted) (pp. 10-14).
positioning: Extends Bertsimas-Lo's single-stock work; the cost split matches Perold's implementation shortfall; cross-autocorrelations from Lo-MacKinlay (pp. 2-3).
writing: A magazine (CiSE) article edited to house style, with a fuller version available (p. 1); sidebars; a concrete 100,000-share example used to judge the fitted impact (p. 10).
limits_future: No error bounds for the static approximation (p. 7). Conclusions are portfolio- and period-specific (p. 14). The claim that the anomalies would vanish with 100,000 replications is not tested (p. 14). Future work: best execution inside portfolio optimization with transaction costs (p. 14).

method_links.note: The baseline is the practitioners' naive equal-lot rule, and the metric is execution cost in cents/share. Calibrated on a partner's proprietary trades (ITG), unlike the simulation-only S009 (card c04). Still scored in simulation with no field test, and the case-specific limit is stated.

The specification is chosen to stay linear-quadratic. The exit from that class is counted (3^k pieces), and the device is changed (a re-solved static QP) rather than the solver. The class is dynamic programming, as in S009 (card c04).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: static methods adapted to dynamic problems
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Instead of the constrained DP, a static convex QP over the remaining horizon is solved from the current state, the first decision implemented, and the problem re-solved each period.

transferable: Count the pieces of the value function once constraints are added (3^k). This shows exactly when the closed-form DP stops being usable, and justifies switching to a QP over the remaining horizon, re-solved each period (p. 6).
Impose the model's well-posedness conditions during estimation (positive definiteness, i.e. no spurious arbitrage) and report the fit given up (about 5% more squared error) (pp. 11-12).
Before using a fitted impact model, test it on one concrete trade, such as a 100,000-share block of one stock (p. 10).

quotes.text: The number of intervals grows exponentially with k.
Of course, these conclusions are highly portfolio- and time-period-specific.

title: Large deviations analysis of the generalized processor sharing policy
contribution: Obtains the large-deviations exponent of buffer overflow under generalized processor sharing, with two classes and stochastic service capacity. The exponent is the value of an explicitly solved optimal-control problem whose optimal trajectories are the most likely ways to overflow, and also the largest root of a convex function.
problem_entry: {SD} Per-class overflow probabilities (about 1e-9) under GPS with bursty traffic. Prior GPS tail results assume deterministic capacity, while stochastic capacity changes how overflows occur (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Write the exponent as the value of a control problem over empirical arrival and service rates (GPS-OVERFLOW), show that two trajectory shapes are optimal, and dualize to get the largest root of a convex function (pp. 7, 9-12, 24-25).
assumptions: Discrete-time fluid model; two classes; infinite buffers; stochastic server; stationary, independent, possibly autocorrelated processes; work-conserving fluid GPS; stability E[B] > E[A1] + E[A2]; Gartner-Ellis and sample-path LD assumptions A-C (pp. 4-7).
proof_devices: Lower bound from two explicit empirical-rate scenarios (Proposition 4.1, pp. 8-9)
Heuristic time scaling to the optimal-control problem with three dynamic regions (pp. 9-11)
One trajectory shape dominates, by monotonicity of rate functions (Theorem 5.1, p. 12)
Matching upper bound (Proposition 6.7, p. 23; proofs not read)
Convex duality: the exponent as the largest positive root of a convex function (Theorem 7.2, pp. 24-25)
Appendix: constant controls within each region (Lemma A.1); time-homogeneity scaling and convexity interchanges reduce all trajectories to two shapes (pp. 26-30)
Priority policies as the special cases phi1 in {0, 1} (Corollaries 7.1, 7.3, pp. 23-26)
positioning: Extends earlier GPS tail results from deterministic to stochastic capacity. Criticizes Courcoubetis-Weber's state-dependent control formulation for boundary problems from its Lipschitz requirement; notes Dupuis-Ramanan. Extends Parekh-Gallager's deterministic worst-case analysis to statistical QoS (pp. 1, 3).
writing: The main theorem is stated up front (Theorem 3.1, p. 7), followed by the lower bound, the control formulation and the upper bound; two contributions named (p. 3); a short conclusion (p. 26).
limits_future: Two streams only; the N-stream case is open (pp. 2, 26). Admission control is named but not developed in the sections read (pp. 1-2). Majewski found a gap in an earlier version (p. 26).

method_links.note: A probability question owned by large-deviations theory is written as an optimal-control problem and dualized into root-finding on a convex function. This is convex analysis with no solver and no computation; the boundary (two classes) is printed. Bears on Inner Tension T3.
The results are included in Paschalidis's 1996 MIT thesis, co-advised with Tsitsiklis (04-mentorship A.2).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: most likely path as an optimizer
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The optimal trajectories of GPS-OVERFLOW are the most likely ways the buffer overflows; also in S177.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: subsume the incumbent as a special case
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Strict priority policies are GPS with phi1 = 1 or 0, and the high-priority case matches the single-class FCFS result.

transferable: Turn a tail-probability exponent into the value of a deterministic control problem over empirical rates. Solve it first over the few trajectory shapes the lower-bound scenarios suggest, then prove those shapes optimal (pp. 9-12, 26-30).
Dualize a constrained rate-function problem so that the exponent becomes the largest root of a convex function, which is easier to compute (Theorem 7.2, pp. 24-25).
In a free-time control problem with convex running cost, take the controls piecewise constant and use scaling (homogeneity) to compare trajectories (Lemma A.1, pp. 26-28).
coauthors: Ioannis Ch. Paschalidis, John N. Tsitsiklis

quotes.text: We view the problem of finding a most likely sample path that leads to an overflow as an optimal control problem.
We have addressed the case of multiplexing two streams. The general case of N streams remains an open problem.

title: Optimization of Multiclass Queueing Networks with Changeover Times Via the Achievable Region Approach: Part I, the Single-Station Case
contribution: Derives new equilibrium constraints for a single-server multiclass queue with changeover times and feedback: Palm-calculus flow conservation valid under changeovers, new work-decomposition laws, server-dynamics and PSD constraints. They give linear, convex and nonconvex lower bounds valid for dynamic policies, recover the buffer-occupancy method as a special case, and suggest heuristic policies.
problem_entry: {SD+LO+CP} A single server with changeovers and Bernoulli feedback. Earlier work analysed specific policies, and changeover-aware bounds existed only for static policies without feedback, so the value of dynamic information could not be judged (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Lift, bound and project with Palm calculus: re-derive Klimov's flow conservation and extend it to changeovers, obtain work-decomposition laws by reformulating flow conservation, add PSD constraints, and solve linear, convex and nonconvex relaxations (pp. 5, 7-9, 14, 20-23).
assumptions: Single server; Poisson arrivals; general service; Bernoulli feedback with I-P invertible; general changeover times; nonanticipative, nonpreemptive, stable policies; steady state (rho < 1 necessary, not sufficient); linear costs; synthetic instances (pp. 3-4, 20).
proof_devices: Palm calculus with a superposition theorem: a new derivation of Klimov's flow-conservation equations, valid with changeovers under any admissible policy (Theorems 1-2, pp. 7-9)
Compact lifted formulation: polynomial size in auxiliary variables versus exponential size in the original variables (zero-changeover case, Remark 1, p. 8)

Work-decomposition laws obtained by reformulating flow-conservation equations; Boxma's law at S = N; new for smaller S, because arrivals during idle periods are not Poisson under feedback (Theorem 5, pp. 14-17)
Linear and convex workload bounds with changeovers (Theorems 6-7, p. 18)

title: Decomposition results for general polling systems and their applications
contribution: Proves decomposition results for polling systems under arbitrary polling order and service policies with non-Poisson arrivals: exact for MGE arrivals, asymptotic in heavy traffic for renewal arrivals. Each queue is related to the same queue in isolation, and the results feed a heavy-traffic analysis of Markovian polling validated by simulation.
problem_entry: {SD} The polling literature is Poisson-based, and its pseudo-conservation laws give only bounds per queue. The paper asks which structural relations hold under general arrivals and policies, and how to use them for performance analysis (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Apply distributional laws to each queue and its waiting room, and condition on whether the server is serving that class. The queue then equals its isolated counterpart combined with a term for the server's absence. Waiting-time decompositions are sharper under static gated or exhaustive policies (pp. 6-7, 12).
assumptions: N classes; one server; renewal arrivals; general service; switch-over delays. A.1-A.4 (FIFO within class, independence); A.5-A.7 for the sharper results (static order, gated or exhaustive, nonzero switch-overs). Exact for MGE arrivals, asymptotic for renewal arrivals in heavy traffic; stability assumed (pp. 1, 3-5, 11).
proof_devices: Vector distributional law for MGE arrivals, plus Little's law at the server and conditioning on the server's presence (Theorems 1-2, pp. 6-7)
Heavy-traffic distributional law from the authors' earlier work (Theorem 5, p. 11), giving Theorems 6-7 (p. 12)
Markovian polling: cycle and intervisit moments from an (N^3+N^2) linear system; a closed form in the symmetric case (pp. 13-18)
Special cases recovered: the isolated queue, cyclic polling, and Kleinrock-Levy random polling extended to general arrivals (pp. 7, 18)
experiments: Five-node Markovian gated polling systems (symmetric and asymmetric), Erlang-2 arrivals, exponential service, d = 0.5 or 2.0, rho 0.5-0.9: heavy-traffic mean waits vs simulation, with standard errors. System-average deviation up to -1.371%; worst per class -7.421% (node 1, rho 0.5). Run lengths not stated; the rho 0.6 row of Table 4 is internally inconsistent (pp. 19-21).
positioning: Set against Poisson-based polling analysis and pseudo-conservation laws (Boxma-Groenendijk, Boxma, Srinivasan et al.); the method is credited to Haji-Newell, Keilson-Servi and the authors' own distributional-law papers (pp. 2-3).
writing: Three numbered contributions, one of them methodological (pp. 2-3); the conclusion restates them and promotes the unified distributional-law approach, without the future directions the introduction promises (pp. 3, 21).
limits_future: Accuracy falls in lighter traffic and for queues with small waits (pp. 20-21). Exact only for MGE arrivals (p. 1). No future directions given (p. 21).

Therefore, they can easily be used to obtain the performance analysis of each queue of the polling system, in contrast with pseudo-conservation laws that can only yield bounds for the individual queues.
